newsitem.title: JAPAN: Thailand says turmoil temporary, no cause for worry.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says turmoil temporary, no cause for worry.

text.p: Thai monetary officials on Friday assured Japanese officials and businessmen that the country's economic turmoil was temporary and no cause for concern, repeating that Bangkok will not seek international aid any time soon.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya and central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond told Japanese business leaders on Friday not to worry because the Thai economy is stable.
Thanong said in a speech that there was no truth in media reports painting a gloomy picture about Thailand's economic development.
"If you trust in these reports, Thailand will be in severe difficulty. There is no truth to these rumours."

Thanong said that after the problems in the financial system are resolved and an equilibrium is established in the exchange market, "domestic interest rates, which were necessarily higher to deter speculative gains, will be lowered to an appropriate level," he said.
Thanong told reporters that the Thai interest rates can be brought down to about 10 percent.

He said that Thailand's export growth, which was about zero last year, is expected to pick up to eight percent this year and 10 percent next year, after a decision was made earlier this month to move to a managed flotation system for the Thai baht.
Thanong also said that Thailand's current account deficit will be reduced to five percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) this year from eight percent last year.

In a meeting earlier with Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, Thanong and Rerngchai explained Bangkok's recent move to a managed flotation system of the Thai baht and recent financial and fiscal steps taken for the economy.
The baht has lost 15-20 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since the de facto devaluation of the Thai currency on July 2.
Mitsuzuka and the Thai officials agreed to cooperate to promote stability in currency markets, with measures including intervention to prop up the baht, Japanese finance ministry officials said.
No request for financial support was made at the meeting, a senior Japanese finance ministry official said.
But Thai officials left open the possibility of asking for global aid in the future.
In a speech delivered to Japanese bankers on Thursday, Thanong said Thailand would ask Japan to join in any international support scheme if it were to call for one.
Bankers said Thai officials held individual meetings with top Japanese bankers during their three-day visit here which ended on Friday.
Some bankers said that Thai officials made specific pleas to individual Japanese bankers, including maintaining a credit line to Thai banks.
But Japanese bankers were wary of giving new money to Thai banks without other global entities chipping in, they said.
Japanese monetary authorities have indicated that a move by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) would be key to Japan's assistance for Thailand.
But on possible financial support from the IMF, Thanong said on Friday: "We have not seen the necessity of getting IMF financing yet."
He added that Thailand is getting technical assistance from the IMF and working closely with the fund.
Thailand's reluctance so far to borrow from the IMF reflects its fear of losing autonomy over economic policies, analysts said.

In order to open a line of credit with the IMF, a country must agree with the fund on its economic policy framework and structural reforms, including tough conditions on spending, balancing trade and controlling inflation.
